crypto.title: Cryptography Track
crypto.subtitle: TechCorp Security Engineer Practical Course
crypto.description: You are a junior security engineer at TechCorp. Across 7 modules you handle one continuous incident: protect a customer backup with symmetric encryption, catch a tampered software release with hashing, harden the login database's password storage, set up RSA for a new partner integration, verify a digital signature, exchange a key with Diffie-Hellman, and close out a real cryptographic incident that combines everything.

module1.title: Symmetric Encryption
module1.mission: Protect a TechCorp customer backup with AES-256-GCM
module1.concept: Symmetric encryption uses ONE shared secret key for both encryption and decryption. It's fast, but both parties must already have the key.

objectives.label:
SCENARIO: TechCorp needs to send a customer backup to a partner system over an untrusted network. As the on-call security engineer, inspect the plaintext before protecting it.

customer_data.txt contents:
"TechCorp customer backup Q3 2026: 4821 records, region=EU-WEST, status=verified"

CONCEPT: Symmetric encryption uses ONE secret key for both encryption and decryption — fast, but both sides must already share that key.

TASK: How many customer records does this backup report? Submit just the number.

CONCEPT: AES-256 uses a 256-bit key. In hex, each byte is 2 characters, so a 256-bit (32-byte) key is 64 hex characters long.

TASK: Generate a real AES-256 key with OpenSSL, then submit how many hex characters it contains (this confirms you understand the key size — not the random value itself, since every engineer's generated key will differ).

TASK: TechCorp already shares a secret key with this specific partner system (key=6f8a3c1e9d4b7f2a5c8e1d4b7a3f6c9e2d5b8a1f4c7e9b2d5a8f1c4e7b9d2a5f, nonce=a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2). Encrypt customer_data.txt with AES-256-GCM using that exact key and nonce. Submit the resulting ciphertext as lowercase hex (authentication tag excluded).
objectives.cmd:
python3 -c "
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
key = bytes.fromhex('6f8a3c1e9d4b7f2a5c8e1d4b7a3f6c9e2d5b8a1f4c7e9b2d5a8f1c4e7b9d2a5f')
nonce = bytes.fromhex('a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2')
pt = open('customer_data.txt','rb').read()
ct = AESGCM(key).encrypt(nonce, pt, None)
print(ct[:-16].hex())"

objectives.label:
Final flag — the partner system sends back this ciphertext (tag=e50423ef9eb279c198b246068bc4f60c):
4e01a7f0af357de45e7da4f2e8cad31e6f141138599822b7d815c52bb11e8d472999da22c9acfe2c9ef0e69e259e1499f1947b715d64af3c1fb63b2bf17c2d98e0c23cb0272921356427b04d656e77

TASK: Decrypt it using the same key and nonce from the previous step, recovering the original plaintext. Submit the recovered plaintext exactly.
objectives.cmd:
python3 -c "
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
key = bytes.fromhex('6f8a3c1e9d4b7f2a5c8e1d4b7a3f6c9e2d5b8a1f4c7e9b2d5a8f1c4e7b9d2a5f')
nonce = bytes.fromhex('a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2')
ct = bytes.fromhex('4e01a7f0af357de45e7da4f2e8cad31e6f141138599822b7d815c52bb11e8d472999da22c9acfe2c9ef0e69e259e1499f1947b715d64af3c1fb63b2bf17c2d98e0c23cb0272921356427b04d656e77') + bytes.fromhex('e50423ef9eb279c198b246068bc4f60c')
print(AESGCM(key).decrypt(nonce, ct, None).decode())"

hints: Hint 1: openssl rand -hex 32 generates a real 256-bit key — count the characters it prints.
Hint 2: AES-256-GCM needs a key, a nonce, and the plaintext; the Python cryptography library's AESGCM class handles the authentication tag automatically.

module2.title: Hash Functions & Integrity
module2.concept: A hash function is one-way and produces a fixed-length digest for any input. It's not encryption — you can't reverse a hash back into the original file.

objectives.label:
SCENARIO: TechCorp just published software_update.bin for customers to download.

CONCEPT: A hash function is one-way (you can't reverse a digest back into the file) and produces a fixed-length digest no matter the input size. This is NOT encryption — there's no key and no decrypting a hash back to the file.

software_update.bin contents:
"TechCorp Update Agent v4.2.0
build=20260824
checksum-protected release binary (simulated)."

TASK: Calculate its SHA-256 hash. This becomes the value TechCorp publishes for customers to verify against.

TASK: A tampered build ("v4.2.1" instead of "v4.2.0" — one character changed) is floating around. Its content:
"TechCorp Update Agent v4.2.1
build=20260824
checksum-protected release binary (simulated)."

Calculate ITS SHA-256 hash too, and compare it by eye to the one from the previous step. Submit this new hash.

TASK — integrity check: TechCorp's official site published this hash for software_update.bin:
a8d85585abd45c7ecbfb01516195ce5ae05984d95d94a98723de3a49868eb260

A partner mirror is serving a copy of the file. Download it, hash it, and compare against the published value. Submit MATCH if the mirror's file is authentic, or MISMATCH if it's been tampered with.
objectives.cmd: sha256sum update_from_mirror.bin  # compare its output to the published hash above

objectives.label: Final flag: which single security property of SHA-256 made it computationally infeasible for the attacker to tamper with the file while keeping the SAME hash? Submit the two-word term (lowercase, e.g. 'x resistance').

hints: Hint 1: sha256sum <file> always prints a 64-character hex digest, no matter the file's size.
Hint 2: If a mirror's hash doesn't match the vendor's published hash, the file has been altered — full stop.

module3.title: Password Hashing
module3.mission: Harden TechCorp's login database against fast-hash attacks
module3.concept: SHA-256 is too fast for password storage — attackers can try billions of guesses per second. Password hashing needs to be deliberately slow (PBKDF2/bcrypt/Argon2) and salted.

objectives.label:
SCENARIO: TechCorp's login database was found storing plain SHA-256(password) — no salt, no slowdown.

CONCEPT: SHA-256 is fast by design, which is exactly wrong for passwords — attackers can hash billions of guesses per second. Password hashing needs to be deliberately SLOW (PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2) and use a per-user SALT so identical passwords don't produce identical hashes.

TASK: What do you add to each password before hashing so two users with the same password get different stored hashes? Submit the one-word term.

TASK: TechCorp is migrating to PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with salt=4f1a9c3e7b2d5f8a and 100000 iterations. Compute the password hash for the candidate password 'Summer2026!'. Submit the resulting hash as lowercase hex.

Final flag: an account's stored hash is:
bbd266be903683b128202b7e6906980df9ce61a5a4c0316b1ee6b50879fe6e90
(salt=4f1a9c3e7b2d5f8a, 100000 iterations, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256)

TASK: One of these candidate passwords is the real one: Winter2025!, TechCorp123, Summer2026!, P@ssw0rd!. Compute each candidate's hash the same way and find the match. Submit the correct password.
objectives.cmd: python3 -c "import hashlib; candidates = ['Winter2025!', 'TechCorp123', 'Summer2026!', 'P@ssw0rd!']; target = 'bbd266be903683b128202b7e6906980df9ce61a5a4c0316b1ee6b50879fe6e90'; salt = bytes.fromhex('4f1a9c3e7b2d5f8a'); [print(c) for c in candidates if hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', c.encode(), salt, 100000).hex() == target]"

hints: Hint 1: hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac('sha256', password_bytes, salt_bytes, iterations) computes PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 in Python.
Hint 2: To find which candidate password is correct, hash each one with the SAME salt and iteration count and compare to the stored hash.

module4.title: Asymmetric Cryptography (RSA)
module4.mission: Generate TechCorp's RSA keypair for a new partner integration
module4.concept: Asymmetric cryptography uses a matched key PAIR: whatever the public key encrypts, only the matching private key can decrypt. The private key never has to be shared.

objectives.label:
SCENARIO: TechCorp's partner integration needs to send a secret value without ever having shared a symmetric key.

CONCEPT: Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography uses a MATCHED PAIR of keys: whatever the PUBLIC key encrypts, only the PRIVATE key can decrypt — and the private key never has to leave TechCorp's server.

TASK: Generate an RSA keypair: given primes p=61 and q=53, compute the modulus n = p x q. This n is shared as part of the PUBLIC key. Submit n.
TASK: Compute phi(n) = (p-1)(q-1) for p=61, q=53. This value is needed to derive the PRIVATE key and must never be published. Submit it.

TASK: TechCorp's public exponent is e=17. Using phi(n)=3120, compute the PRIVATE exponent d — the modular inverse of e mod phi(n), satisfying (e x d) mod phi(n) = 1. This d, kept secret on TechCorp's server, is the private key. Submit d.

Final flag: put TechCorp's PUBLIC key to work. Using n=3233 and e=17, encrypt the partner's secret value m=88 by computing c = m^e mod n. This is exactly what the partner does with TechCorp's public key — they never need the private key to send a message only TechCorp can read. Submit c as FLAG{{c}}.

hints: Hint 1: n = p*q and phi(n) = (p-1)*(q-1) are simple arithmetic once you have the primes.
Hint 2: Python's pow(e, -1, phi_n) computes the modular inverse directly — that's your private exponent d.

module5.title: Digital Signatures
module5.mission: Confirm update.bin really came from TechCorp, unmodified
module5.concept: A signature is created with the PRIVATE key and checked with the PUBLIC key — proving both who signed something and that it hasn't changed since.

objectives.label:
SCENARIO: TechCorp's release team published update.bin along with a digital signature and their public key. Your job is to confirm the update really came from TechCorp and wasn't altered.

CONCEPT: A digital signature flips RSA around: you sign with your PRIVATE key so ANYONE can verify with your PUBLIC key. It proves both authenticity (who signed it) and integrity (it hasn't changed since).

TASK: Using TechCorp's private key (d=2753, n=3233 from Module 4), sign the release's hash-digest stand-in h=15 by computing s = h^d mod n. Submit s — this is the signature TechCorp attaches to update.bin.

TASK: Verify the signature the way any customer could, using only TechCorp's PUBLIC key: compute h' = s^e mod n with e=17, n=3233, and signature s=452. If h' equals update.bin's real hash-digest (15), the signature is valid. Submit h'.

TASK: An attacker now modifies update.bin after it was signed. The modified file's hash-digest is now 22 instead of 15 — but the attacker kept the ORIGINAL signature (452), since they don't have TechCorp's private key to forge a new one.

Verify the SAME signature against the NEW (tampered) hash-digest. Does it still check out? Submit VALID or INVALID.

Final flag: which single property did this whole exercise demonstrate — the one guaranteeing a signed file can't be silently modified without breaking verification? Submit one word: 'integrity', 'confidentiality', or 'availability'.

hints: Hint 1: Signing and decrypting use the identical formula: value^d mod n. Verifying and encrypting both use value^e mod n.
Hint 2: If the file changes after signing, its hash-digest changes too — but the OLD signature only verifies against the OLD digest.

module6.title: Key Exchange (Diffie-Hellman)
module6.mission: Agree on a shared secret with a brand-new partner system
module6.concept: Diffie-Hellman lets two sides who've never met derive the same shared secret over a public channel, without ever transmitting the secret itself.

objectives.label:
SCENARIO: TechCorp is integrating with a brand-new partner system. Neither side has ever shared a secret key, and there's no secure channel yet to send one over.

CONCEPT: Diffie-Hellman lets two sides agree on a shared secret over a channel an attacker can freely watch, without ever transmitting the secret itself.

TASK: Both sides publicly agree on prime p=23 and generator g=5. TechCorp picks private value a=6 and computes its public value A = g^a mod p. Submit A (safe to publish — this is the 'public value' side of the exchange).
TASK: The partner system picks its own private value b=15 and computes its public value B = g^b mod p. Submit B.
TASK: TechCorp now combines the PARTNER's public value (B=19) with its OWN private value (a=6): shared = B^a mod p. Submit the shared secret TechCorp derives.

Final flag: now compute it from the PARTNER's side: combine TechCorp's public value (A=8) with the partner's own private value (b=15): shared = A^b mod p. Submit this value — it should exactly match what TechCorp derived, proving both sides landed on the same shared secret without ever transmitting it.

hints: Hint 1: Both public values are computed the same way: pow(g, private_value, p).
Hint 2: The shared secret is pow(their_public_value, your_private_value, p) — both sides land on the identical number.

module7.title: Final Incident: Verify & Recover
module7.mission: Investigate and close a real cryptographic incident end-to-end
module7.concept: Real incident response always verifies BEFORE trusting: check integrity (hash), check authenticity (signature), and only then decrypt and act on the data.

objectives.label:
FINAL INCIDENT: TechCorp received an encrypted customer backup (backup.enc) from a partner server, along with a published hash and a claim it was properly signed. Your job as the security engineer on call: verify it, then recover the data.

TASK — Step 1, verify integrity: the partner published this hash out-of-band for the backup's plaintext:
1692b4ee2bd6bf14cc1f52759ed7efd6cdfe274677004f4f881bcf8b0889ff05

The backup's actual plaintext (once decrypted) is provided below for this hash check:
"INCIDENT-CLOSED: partner backup TC-9471 verified and recovered successfully"

Hash it and confirm it matches. Submit MATCH or MISMATCH.
objectives.cmd: echo -n "INCIDENT-CLOSED: partner backup TC-9471 verified and recovered successfully" | sha256sum

objectives.label: TASK — Step 2, verify the sender: the partner claims this backup's hash-digest (15) was signed with their private key, producing signature 452 (reusing the keypair from Modules 4-5: n=3233, e=17). Verify it the same way as Module 5: compute h' = s^e mod n and confirm it matches. Submit VALID or INVALID.

TASK — Step 3, decrypt the backup: now that it's verified, decrypt backup.enc using AES-256-GCM with key=1c9e4a7f2b8d5e3c6a9f4b7d2e8c5a1f9b4e7d2a8c5f1b9e4d7a2c8f5b1e9d4a, nonce=f0e1d2c3b4a5968778695a4b, ciphertext=f74deaf7d1605abe57847ccc1f9a53ce2d3f9c3c2eaea72207569592a5a71d6867cec1010c6f46c9abb88ee4b861a0496e268d5b06cc84511d30b5e1d2623db593564c45aca6b64ef1402c, tag=d61e4da10998b899f2c9c6945ff15415. Submit the recovered plaintext exactly.
objectives.cmd:
python3 -c "
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
key = bytes.fromhex('1c9e4a7f2b8d5e3c6a9f4b7d2e8c5a1f9b4e7d2a8c5f1b9e4d7a2c8f5b1e9d4a')
nonce = bytes.fromhex('f0e1d2c3b4a5968778695a4b')
ct = bytes.fromhex('f74deaf7d1605abe57847ccc1f9a53ce2d3f9c3c2eaea72207569592a5a71d6867cec1010c6f46c9abb88ee4b861a0496e268d5b06cc84511d30b5e1d2623db593564c45aca6b64ef1402c') + bytes.fromhex('d61e4da10998b899f2c9c6945ff15415')
print(AESGCM(key).decrypt(nonce, ct, None).decode())"

objectives.label: FINAL FLAG: you've now completed the full incident — integrity check, signature verification, and decryption. Submit the case status exactly as it should be logged, wrapped as FLAG{...} (see the recovered plaintext above for the exact case ID and status).

hints: Hint 1: Work the steps in order — hash check, then signature check, then decrypt. Don't decrypt first.
Hint 2: Reuse the exact AES-256-GCM and RSA-verification approach from Modules 1 and 5 — the mechanics are identical, only the values differ.
